request: Check this flight: did a control fault occur, when, and where on the aircraft?

result.headline: Pitch-axis control loss from t≈119 s; actuator ch[2] and pitch diverged, altitude fell 57 to 36 m.
result.explanation: Pitch responded opposite to the setpoint at t=120-122, then overshot to -30 deg and +33 deg. Actuator ch[2], which drives pitch and throttle, saturated. The cause is not separated between a ch[2] actuator or pitch-loop fault and an external disturbance.

evidence.shows: Pitch rose about 8 deg before any command change. Before this the loop tracked within a few degrees.
The nose went up while the setpoint was nose down. The same ch[2] command at t=2-3 gave the correct response (pitch -12.8, then -21.7).
Pitch overshot to nose down by about 25 deg, then stayed negative while ch[2] rose to 1680 and throttle to 75%.
Altitude fell about 20 m after peaking at 58.6 m at t=122.
The aircraft was still unstable at the end of the log, with pitch +33 deg and roll 30 deg.

checked.check: Pitch tracking before t=119 compared with t=119-128
checked.result: Pitch followed its setpoint within about 5 deg for t=4-118, including repeated 45 deg roll turns. It diverged from t=119.

checked.check: Which channels move with the fault
checked.result: Only ch[2] and the throttle moved sharply, which places the fault on the pitch axis. ch[1], ch[3], ch[4] and ch[5] barely moved, ch[4] and ch[5] are identical throughout, and ch[0], ch[6] and ch[7] are constant.

checked.check: Roll and yaw behaviour at t=119-128
checked.result: Roll stayed within about 13 deg until t=127 and heading was steady near 635-640 deg, so the fault is pitch-specific.
Both are 0 for the whole flight while ground speed is about 15-20 m/s and heading changes. They are dead or not logged.

effects.why: Altitude loss follows from the pitch and throttle excursion.
Throttle saturation looks like the controller reacting to the pitch and altitude error.
The late roll excursion follows the pitch upset.

next_action.action: Inspect the ch[2] actuator, linkage and pitch estimator, and replay the t=115-128 s log
next_action.why: Separates a ch[2] actuator or linkage fault, a pitch-estimate fault and an external disturbance as the cause of the pitch divergence.
how: Compare ch[2] commanded output with measured actuator position or feedback, if it is logged
Check the IMU pitch against the attitude estimate for t=115-128
Bench-test ch[2] response and direction across its full range
next_action.conditions: Bench test with the vehicle disarmed and propellers removed; replay the log with the same control gains.
next_action.baseline: Compare with the earlier correct pitch response at t=1-4 s for the same ch[2] command.

outcomes.label: ch[2] response is wrong or sluggish
outcomes.means: Actuator, linkage or ESC fault on ch[2] is the main cause.
outcomes.then: Replace the ch[2] actuator or linkage and retest

outcomes.label: Actuator is fine, estimator pitch disagrees with IMU
outcomes.means: The pitch estimate was faulty, so the controller acted on a wrong pitch.
outcomes.then: Review the estimator and IMU health logs

unknowns: Whether ch[2] is a throttle, elevator or thrust-vectoring output; the data does not label it.
Whether wind or a gust acted at t≈119; no wind data is in the log.

already_answered.question: When did the control fault start?
already_answered.answer: Pitch started to diverge at about t=119-120 s, after more than 100 s of normal tracking.

already_answered.question: Which axis and channel was affected?
already_answered.answer: The pitch axis, with the large swings on actuator ch[2] and throttle.

unobservable.fact: Physical condition and direction of the ch[2] actuator or linkage
unobservable.why_it_matters: Separates an actuator fault from an estimator or disturbance cause.
unobservable.how_to_observe: Inspect the actuator and bench-test its travel and direction.

hypotheses.claim: Pitch control through ch[2] failed or reversed at about t=119-120, causing the pitch divergence and altitude loss.
hypotheses.because: The pitch response was opposite to the setpoint with the same ch[2] command that worked early in the flight; roll and yaw were unaffected.

hypotheses.claim: The pitch estimate was faulty, so the controller acted on a wrong pitch.
hypotheses.because: The data cannot separate it from an actuator fault, and the airspeed and yaw-rate channels are dead, so sensor health is already poor.

hypotheses.claim: The airspeed and yaw-rate signals are dead, as the sensor-health error at t=0.3 s suggests.
hypotheses.because: Airspeed and yaw rate are 0 for the whole flight. Normal flight continued until t=119, so this did not directly cause the divergence.

hypotheses.claim: A gust or aerodynamic disturbance pushed the nose up at about t=119.
hypotheses.because: The pitch rise preceded the command change, but there is no wind data to confirm it.

events.what: Low battery voltage warning at t=0.3 s
events.why: Battery warning at the start of the flight; no related change is visible in the data.

events.what: System error 'Sensor helth' at t=0.3 s
events.why: Consistent with airspeed and yaw-rate reading 0 for the whole flight.

events.what: Pitch rises as throttle drops to 3%
events.why: Start of the pitch divergence and the opposite-sign response.

events.what: Pitch -30 to +33 deg, altitude 57 to 36 m
events.why: Pitch oscillation and altitude loss following the upset.

result.reuse_when: A pitch response opposite to its setpoint on a channel that previously tracked well, with the airspeed and yaw-rate channels dead and a sensor-health error at flight start.
